summary:
Evarínya is a free web tool that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change over time, using real images from NASA's SPHEREx mission. You pick a target or type in sky coordinates, and Evarínya finds every SPHEREx image of that spot, cleans , aligns them, and plays them as a time-lapse so you can spot what moves or changes. It also offers a difference view, where fixed stars cancel and moving objects stand out in red and blue, and it draws the expected path of fast-moving stars and brown dwarfs.

It answers the SPHEREx challenge by turning raw archive data into something anyone can explore without knowing FITS files or archive queries. Our addition is automatic colour selection: SPHEREx sees the sky in six infrared colours, so Evarínya measures the signal-to-noise at your target in each one, picks the clearest, and explains the choice in a sentence.

It matters because NASA's all-sky survey is hard for newcomers to approach. Evarínya opens it up to students, teachers and curious people, and it is honest about its limits, labelling results as candidates rather than confirmed discoveries.
details:
What it does and how it works

Evarínya is a free web tool for watching the infrared sky change over time in real NASA SPHEREx images. You pick an example target (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis), search a name, or type RA/Dec coordinates. Behind the scenes it:

• asks NASA/IPAC's archive (IRSA) which SPHEREx exposures cover that spot

• downloads small cutouts of each exposure

• removes zodiacal light, masks bad pixels, and aligns every image on one north-up grid

• optionally stacks images taken close in time to reduce noise

You can then:

• play the time-lapse

• flip between the earliest and latest image

• open a difference image where fixed stars cancel and moving or changing objects show up in red (brighter later) and blue (brighter earlier)

SPHEREx observes in six infrared "colours", so Evarínya also:

• measures the signal-to-noise at your target in each colour, picks the clearest automatically, and explains the choice in one sentence (you can override it)

• draws the expected path of fast-moving objects from their proper motion

• builds a rough spectrum of the spot

• flags bright peaks as possible sources, always as candidates, never confirmed objects

• creates a shareable link for every view

Benefits

• Anyone can explore real SPHEREx data without knowing FITS files or archive queries.

• Automatic colour selection spares beginners from noisy images.

• It is honest about its limits, labelling results as candidates and warning when frames differ in wavelength.

• It is light and quick, using small cutouts and caching.

Intended impact

We want to make NASA's all-sky infrared survey approachable for students, teachers and curious people. It helps them spot fast-moving stars and brown dwarfs by eye, and learn how infrared colour reveals what an object is.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

• Language and app: Python, with Streamlit for the app and Plotly for the interactive animation

• Libraries: Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Reproject, PyVO, Requests, Pillow

• Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 wide-survey spectral images), and SIMBAD for names and proper motions

• Platform: GitHub and streamlit https://evarinya-spherex.streamlit.app/

• Hardware: ordinary laptops, with no special hardware

• AI use: Claude (Anthropic) and GitHub Copilot helped write and debug code and documentation, and helped us learn the science. The team chose the approach, and ran, tested and checked the results.

How it is creative

• The challenge asks for a time-lapse. We added automatic best-colour selection with a plain-language explanation.

• The difference view and proper-motion overlay make motion easy to see, not just a flip-book.

• Everything is written for beginners.

• It says "candidate" and shows its limits rather than overclaiming.

Factors our team considered

• Each frame is at a slightly different wavelength, so a star can change brightness without being variable.

• SPHEREx pixels are 6.15 arcseconds wide, so motion of a few arcseconds per year is only about one pixel.

• Very bright stars saturate, and very faint ones disappear in a single exposure.

• Catalogue positions are for the year 2000, so fast movers need proper-motion correction.

• The photometry is rough, so it suits comparing colours, not measuring absolute brightness.

• We credited all data and tools and disclosed our AI use.
dataRefs: SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 data (NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive)
